title: Stoic at home
hook: the hive, the household, the people you live with

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoic at work, two columns and the fitting thing. Your line was my part at work. Did you do the one thing from the left column? Day six hundred seventy-eight.

The sink has a pan in it that's been soaking since Tuesday. Nobody remembers whose it is. It's become a sort of household monument. Everyone walks past it. Everyone has an opinion about it. Nobody touches it. If you've lived with other people, roommates, a partner, kids, parents, you know this pan, or its cousin, the empty toilet paper roll. It's funny how hard it can be to be patient and good in the place where we're most ourselves. The Stoics thought home was exactly where philosophy gets tested. Today: Stoic at home.
screen: `THE PAN SOAKING SINCE TUESDAY.` → `EVERYONE WALKS PAST IT.` → `WHERE PHILOSOPHY GETS TESTED.`

segments.voice: First, the hive. Marcus Aurelius writes, in George Long's 1862 translation: "That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee." One line, and a whole picture. A bee doesn't thrive by doing well while the hive falls apart. Whatever helps only me, at the expense of the people I live with, isn't really good for me either. Second, the circles. A later Stoic named Hierocles drew a picture that Stoic readers still use. Imagine yourself at the center of a set of circles. The first ring is your own mind and body. The next is your closest family, then your wider family, neighbors, your town, and finally all of humanity. The task, he says, is to draw the circles inward: to treat the people in each ring a little more like the ones closer in. And the household is the very first ring past your own skin. Third, the Stoic word underneath. Oikeiōsis: making something your own, belonging. It comes from oikos, the Greek word for household. For the Stoics, our care starts at home and grows outward from there. Home isn't a break from virtue. It's where virtue learns to walk. Fourth, the pan. In practice, a Stoic at home isn't someone who never gets annoyed. It's someone who asks, what's good for the hive? And then does one small thing for it without keeping score. Wash the pan. Replace the roll. Not as a martyr, not as a point being made. Just as a bee who knows where it lives.
screen: `NOT GOOD FOR THE SWARM, NOR THE BEE.` · `HIEROCLES' CIRCLES, DRAWN INWARD.` · `OIKEIŌSIS: FROM OIKOS, HOUSEHOLD.` · `ONE THING FOR THE HIVE, NO SCORE.` · then, large: `FOR THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Picture your home and the people in it, or if you live alone, the people closest to you. See each face. Now picture the circles: you in the middle, then them. Notice whether there's any score being kept, about chores, about who gives more. Just notice; no blame. Then choose one small thing you could do for the house today, something nobody asked for. Picture yourself doing it quietly, without announcing it. The bell holds the time.
Stoic at home: treating the household as the hive and the first circle, and doing your part for it without keeping score. Today's word.
Your line: for the house. Do the one small thing you chose, and don't mention it. Let the house just be a little better. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat the household as the first circle of their care, doing small unasked tasks for the people they live with without keeping score.

original.note: Greek, Stoic term: making one's own, belonging; from oikos, household.

trapdoor: what you thought: being Stoic at home means staying calm about the mess.
what it means: treating the household as your first circle and the hive you belong to, and doing your part for it.
what a scholar hears: Meditations 6.54 on the swarm and the bee; Hierocles' concentric circles survive in Stobaeus; oikeiōsis, the Stoic theory of appropriation, shares a root with oikos.
